chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
title: Day job as assistant engineer at Western while playing nights
summary: Married with a child, he took a $45-60 a month job at Western and played 8-to-4 clubs, napping in the boiler room.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Well, then, you know, now when you're working with her now, are you still at the college?
I'm still at Western University, as Assistant Engineer.
Oh.
See, I've graduated now, and I took a job there as Assistant Engineer.
Well, what did you have to do?

Well, I was more or less a superintendent of some sort. We had to repair--they had a laundry on the place, and there was a 300-volt current there. And the irons were naturally 110, and we had to help with the generators and the transistors--whatever you call them--
--transformers--
--transformers, yeah.
Well, so you took that for the money, I take it?
Well, by that time, I was married and had a child, see.
Oh.
And that was more secure than the music because--I, actually I was only making $45.00--I finally went up to $60.00 a month, at Western University.
$60.00 a month?
Yeah.
Wow!
And so--
But you had living quarters, I take it?
No. I was buying a home.
(chuckles) Well, how could you do that even then?
Well, that's why I had to get that other job.
Oh, yeah, with the music, huh?
With the music. I was gettin' very little sleep. I'd get home at 5:00 o'clock, and--
Well, what hours did you work, with the band?

Those clubs on 12th Street-- they were 8 to 4, sometime 8 to 5. And those clubs--the man usually wouldn't let you quit. He wouldn't let me quit. And although I already had that job at Western University, I took the job in the music, you know, that steady job. But I'd gone with Todd in the winter of 1935. We opened at a place called Frankie's and Johnny's. A man wasn't even able to buy a--to pay for the heat. So we played there with overcoats on. (chuckle)
Well, yeah, so I mean do you come

Yeah, somethin' like three, two or three. See, being as talented as I most honourably am, see, I have found a very nice thing to do. I'd get down to that boiler room, I'd stuff that thing (laughter)--full with coal and go to sleep.

Oh, yeah. Sometime I would sleep like five hours a day. Somebody'd come running down there and say, "Listen, all the buildings are cold!" (laughter) Well, I'd be so sleepy that--and I did that until '37.
